column6: The Hebrew verb yādîn, “he will judge,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic d-y-n; here YHWH judges his people and vindicates them against their oppressors.
The Aramaic court term dînâ is cognate with Arabic dīn; in the same verse the court sits and books are opened, so the cognate occurs in a concrete judgment scene.
Hebrew melekh, “king,” is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k; Isaiah uses it for the Lord beside “judge” and “lawgiver.”
Hebrew yôm is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic y-w-m; this verse says day and night belong to God and names the appointed light and sun.
The commentary lets mālik carry both possession and rule; Isaiah places the Lord’s judicial, legislative, royal, and saving roles in one verse.

column5: All things and kingship belong to God
column6: David’s prayer assigns everything in heaven and earth, and the kingdom itself, to God; this makes human ownership provisional beside the Day’s sole owner.
Abraham asks whether the judge of all the earth will do what is just; the universal jurisdiction gives the commentary’s judgment day a concrete biblical counterpart.
Within Moses’ song, God reserves vengeance and repayment for the appointed time; this links the day’s closing account with a reckoning that no human claimant controls.
The law says parents and children die for their own offenses, not one another’s; it parallels the commentary’s day when no person can own or pay another’s account.
At the close of Ecclesiastes, God brings every deed to judgment, even what is concealed; this matches the commentary’s expansion from public evidence to inward acts.
Elihu says God repays a person according to what that person has done; the direct correspondence is the commentary’s account settled in full on the owned day.
The Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to conduct; this connects the commentary’s private intention and heart-accounting with an explicit biblical judgment formula.
Hannah says the Lord weighs actions; this gives the commentary’s image of an unbending scale a moral use, not merely a lexical association with measure.

column5: Just scales belong to the Lord
column6: Proverbs says honest balances and weights are the Lord’s; the commentary likewise makes the final account a measure whose standard belongs to the day’s owner.
Daniel interprets the king’s writing as a verdict that he was weighed and found deficient; it turns the commentary’s balance image into a royal judgment scene.
Daniel sees the court seated and books opened before the Ancient of Days; this closely matches the commentary’s tribunal, record, witnesses, and full payment of deeds.
Malachi records the words of those who fear the Lord in a book before him; the written record parallels the commentary’s books that preserve what people did.
WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; in English numbering this is Psalm 49:7. The singer says no person can ransom a brother from death, matching the day when no one can pay another’s due.
Job says he came naked from the womb and will return naked; this sharpens the commentary’s image of property and servants left behind when a person comes alone.

column5: The dead awake to opposed destinies
column6: Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening to everlasting life or disgrace; it supplies resurrection and final outcome for the commentary’s day of reckoning.
Zephaniah calls the Lord’s day near and bitter, a day of battle cries; the day is an approaching event that overtakes people, as the commentary emphasizes.
Isaiah pictures the heavens rolled up like a scroll as the host falls; this matches the commentary’s cosmic unmaking, in which the sky can no longer serve as a clock.
Joel’s day of the Lord darkens the sun and moon and shakes the heavens; the signs make the commentary’s judgment day exceed ordinary solar measurement.
Amos announces darkness at midday as judgment on Israel; unlike the final day in the commentary, this is a historical oracle, but it makes the solar clock fail at the moment of reckoning.
WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 90:4. A thousand years are like yesterday before God, matching the commentary’s day whose measure is not the sun’s daily course.
The vision waits for its appointed time and will not fail to arrive; this connects the commentary’s “falling/coming event” sense of the day with an event whose date is delayed but certain.
The prophet says the day of the watchmen and punishment has come amid social collapse; Micah’s next verses name betrayal within households, echoing the commentary’s day when ties fail.
Son, daughter, and daughter-in-law turn against close kin; in Micah this follows the announced day of punishment, a concrete social image for the commentary’s fleeing family bonds.
Zechariah commands true justice and mercy, then forbids oppressing widow, orphan, stranger, and poor; this joins the commentary’s judgment day to its contrast between mercy and punishment.
The same verse also works as a motif: day, night, sun, and light are under God’s ordering, making time itself part of the sovereignty the commentary assigns to the Day.

column5: Judge who feeds and clothes the vulnerable
column6: God executes justice for orphan and widow and gives food and clothing to the stranger; this connects the commentary’s merciful owner with concrete care for those who lack worldly power.
Sirach says God judges without favoritism and hears the wronged, orphan, and widow; this puts mercy toward the vulnerable inside the same final-account framework as the commentary.

column5: All are God’s and spared by mercy
column6: Wisdom says God loves what exists and spares it because it is his; this joins the commentary’s ownership language to the mercy that precedes its judgment title.
The midrash says creation could not stand by strict justice alone, so mercy was placed first and justice joined to it; this illuminates Fatiha’s sequence of Rahman/Rahim before the Day of judgment.
Akavya tells each person to consider where they came from, where they go, and before whom they will give account; it gives the commentary’s solitary arrival a Jewish ethical formulation.
The shopkeeper gives credit, the ledger is open, and collectors regularly collect; the image makes the commentary’s debt, record, due date, and final repayment unusually concrete.

column5: Judgment before the King of Kings
column6: The saying pairs unavoidable death with judgment before the King of Kings, matching the commentary’s sovereign who owns the day and the account due then.
The Talmud pictures three books opened on Rosh Hashanah for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate; it develops the commentary’s book-and-verdict image into a graded inscription tradition.

The Talmud’s questions at judgment include whether one dealt faithfully in business and pursued wisdom; this makes ordinary habits part of the account, as the commentary says sustained conduct is judged.

column5: Throne and books of the living
column6: Enoch sees the Head of Days on his throne as the books of the living are opened; this is a close Jewish apocalyptic court scene for the commentary’s records and final accounting.
At the world’s end the Most High appears on the judgment seat and recompense follows; this parallels the commentary’s day when the account is complete and no earthly claim can alter it.
The prayer addresses God as “Our Father, our King” and asks for inscription in the book of life; it holds royal sovereignty and hoped-for mercy together in a judgment-season setting.

column5: The Son of Man enthroned as King
column6: Jesus’ discourse places the glorious Son of Man on a throne before the nations are judged; it gives the commentary’s “owner of the day” a concrete royal court scene.
The king separates people as a shepherd sorts sheep from goats; this joins the commentary’s day of division to its image of a leader whose destination determines the followers’ fate.

At judgment, giving drink to a thirsty person is evidence of mercy; the commentary instead shows condemned people asking for water and being refused, so the shared water scene exposes opposite outcomes.
The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus with water for his burning tongue; this closely matches the commentary’s damned who call across the divide for water.
Abraham says a great chasm prevents passage between the two sides; it explains why the water plea in Luke cannot be met and parallels the commentary’s closed access to the saved community’s water.
The king has compassion and releases a servant by cancelling his enormous debt; this is a specific Christian image for the commentary’s owner who can forgive what is owed on the day of settlement.
The Son of Man comes in glory and repays each person according to conduct; it directly matches the commentary’s account fully paid to every person.
Paul says God judges people’s secrets through Christ; this is a precise bridge to the commentary’s claim that hidden intentions enter the final account.
Paul says all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat to receive for what was done in the body; it joins individual embodiment and deeds to the commentary’s personal reckoning.
The author says no creature is concealed and all are exposed before the one to whom account must be given; this matches the commentary’s turn from public records to the heart’s hidden contents.

column5: Books opened and the dead judged
column6: John sees the dead judged by what is written in opened books, each according to deeds; this is a close Christian counterpart to the commentary’s court, records, and full recompense.
After Babylon’s fall, the heavenly crowd praises God because his judgments are true and just; this parallels the commentary’s praise formula voiced after judgment is completed.

column5: Sun and moon lose their light
column6: The sun turns dark and the moon like blood as the day of wrath unfolds; this matches the commentary’s judgment scene in which the sun ceases to measure the day.

column5: Sky rolls up like a scroll
column6: John sees the sky vanish like a rolled scroll; this is a close image for the commentary’s cosmic collapse and the end of ordinary celestial order.
Peter compares a day before the Lord to a thousand years; this makes explicit the commentary’s contrast between solar days and divine time.

column5: An appointed day and righteous judgment
column6: Paul says God fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness, with resurrection as assurance; the verse directly links day, divine judgment, and resurrection.
James says judgment is without mercy for one who has shown no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this holds the commentary’s mercy and wrath together as an ethical test.

John says the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son; this differs from the commentary’s emphasis on God as sole owner and final judge by assigning the court’s execution to a distinct divine figure.

column5: Christ intercedes at God’s right hand
column6: Paul identifies the risen Christ as intercessor; beside the commentary’s speech and intercession available only by the Rahman’s leave, this gives that permitted role a specific Christian mediator.
The doxology calls God the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords; it complements the commentary’s distinction between possession and rule by declaring ultimate royal authority.

column5: Stored wealth cannot accompany the dead
column6: God tells the rich fool that his life is demanded that night and asks who will own his stores; this dramatizes the commentary’s claim that worldly property stays behind when a person comes alone.
Paul says the trumpet sounds and the dead are raised imperishable; this supplies the resurrection event behind the commentary’s final-day accounting.
The author links death once with judgment afterward; this brings the commentary’s deathbed scene and the day of account into one sequence.

column5: Patristic reading of the last judgment
column6: Augustine’s discussion of the final judgment around Revelation 20 treats it as a public reckoning of the dead; it gives the commentary’s opened court and day-as-event a major Christian interpretive frame.

column5: The King’s judgment measured by mercy
column6: Chrysostom’s homily on Matthew 25 reads feeding and giving drink to the needy as the King’s criterion at judgment; it clarifies the ethical weight of the commentary’s denied water and neglected poor.

The hymn imagines the judge arriving, the trumpet summoning the dead, and a written record disclosing deeds; it gathers the commentary’s day, resurrection, and account into Christian liturgical language.

The next verse names widow, orphan, stranger, and poor and forbids plotting harm against one another; it makes Zechariah’s justice-and-mercy command concrete, as the commentary links final belief to how the weak are treated.

column5: Kings and times given or removed
column6: Daniel’s prayer says God changes times, removes kings, and raises kings; this directly supports the commentary’s point that worldly possession and rule are granted and withdrawn by the day’s true sovereign.

Isaiah asks who measured the waters in the hollow of a hand, marked the heavens, and weighed mountains; this gathers the commentary’s strong grasp, water, cosmic ownership, and scale into one biblical image.

WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 23:2. The Lord leads the speaker to waters of rest, matching the commentary’s meeting of guide, path, and water that sustains a traveler.

Jesus contrasts the broad road to destruction with the narrow way to life; this gives a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary’s path-center, guidance, and danger of following a misleading route.

column5: The Lamb guides to living water
column6: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water; this brings the commentary’s leading guide and life-sustaining water together in an eschatological scene.
Jesus’ parable says neither debtor can pay, so the creditor cancels both debts; this illuminates the commentary’s image of the Day’s owner as a creditor able to forgive what is owed.
The Lord’s Prayer asks God to forgive debts as worshippers forgive their debtors; it links the commentary’s debt-account sense of dīn with the ethical practice of releasing another’s claim.
The verse says each believer will give an account of himself to God; it is a direct New Testament parallel to the commentary’s day when no one can answer or pay for another.

column5: Hidden purposes of the heart revealed
column6: Paul says the Lord will expose what is hidden in darkness and disclose the heart’s purposes; this closely matches the commentary’s inner account that public records cannot exhaust.

column5: Trumpet and raising of the dead
column6: At the last trumpet the dead are raised imperishable; this supplies a Christian resurrection scene for the commentary’s final day and the transition from death to account.
Daniel’s Aramaic malkû names the enduring kingdom given to the humanlike figure; it is cognate with the commentary’s labeled Arabic m-l-k and appears in a scene where all peoples serve the ruler.

God names himself compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in covenant love; this is a close biblical pairing for the commentary’s Rahman/Rahim immediately before the title “owner of the Day.”
The same self-revelation says God forgives wrongdoing yet does not simply clear the guilty; this preserves both mercy and accountability in the sequence the commentary develops.
The proverb asks whether the one who weighs hearts will not know, then says he repays each according to work; it joins hidden motives to exact recompense in one passage.

column5: The Lord comes to judge the world
column6: The psalm says the Lord comes to judge earth and peoples with righteousness; creation’s response makes this a compact scene of universal judgment, not just a shared “day” word.
The next verse after Zephaniah’s approaching day names distress, darkness, and a trumpet blast; it adds the day’s sensory and cosmic disturbance to the commentary’s non-solar event.

WLC numbering includes the psalm heading; this is English Psalm 103:10. The psalm says God has not treated people according to their sins, a concrete counterweight to the commentary’s full repayment and merciful creditor.
Abraham’s vision shows a soul assessed by its deeds on a balance; this is a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary’s upright scale and final account.

column5: Prayer and offering for the dead
column6: Judas arranges atonement for fallen soldiers in hope that they may be freed from sin; this gives a different account of aid across death from the commentary’s claim that no one can pay another’s due.

column4: Unetanneh Tokef, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur liturgy
column5: Creatures pass before the King and records seal fate
column6: The prayer pictures all creatures passing before God, with life and death written and sealed; it extends the commentary’s sovereign day, personal account, and written verdict in a Jewish liturgical setting.

The kings and mighty see the Son of Man on the throne and are overcome with fear while the righteous stand before him; this adds the commentary’s royal sovereignty and the collapse of worldly rank to Enoch’s court scene.
Jesus says people will give account on the day of judgment for careless words; this gives a concrete relation between the commentary’s loss of speech-rights and the court’s accounting.

column5: The day’s date is not disclosed
column6: Jesus says no one knows the day or hour; alongside the commentary’s answer to “when?” by describing what happens rather than naming a date, it keeps the reader’s attention on the event and readiness.

Peter says all will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead; this gathers the commentary’s death scene, universal judgment, and personal accounting in a concise Christian formulation.

column5: Death and Hades release their dead
column6: The next verse after John’s opened books says sea, Death, and Hades give up the dead for judgment; it adds the gathering of every person from death’s custody to the commentary’s tribunal scene.
